title: USGS NWIS annual statistics, mean daily discharge, Great Salt Lake tributaries (Bear River near Corinne 10126000; Weber River near Plain City 10141000; Surplus Canal at Salt Lake City 10170490; Jordan River 10172630)
authors: U.S. Geological Survey
publisher: U.S. Geological Survey, National Water Information System (water services statistics API)
location: RDB output, column mean_va, water years 1943-2025
conversion: Parsed annual mean daily discharge (mean_va, cfs) from the four RDB files. Converted each to acre-feet/yr with x723.97 and summed the three long-record gauges (Bear R nr Corinne 10126000, Weber R nr Plain City 10141000, Surplus Canal 10170490) over their 69 common years 1950-2025 (1957-1963 missing). python3 -I: mean=1,875,736 AF/yr, sd=1,189,548, CV=sd/mean=0.634. AR(1)=sum((x_t-m)(x_t+1-m))/sum((x_t-m)^2) over the 67 consecutive pairs = 0.526 (0.510 in log space). Jordan R at 10172630 has only 34 non-contiguous years so it was excluded from the combined series; its own CV is 1.036. Per-gauge CV/AR1 over full records: 10126000 0.621/0.492, 10141000 0.817/0.424, 10170490 0.712/0.728. Driest 20-year running mean (2003-2022) = 1,372,061 AF/yr = 0.731 of the 69-year mean.
differencesFromUtah: None: this is the Great Salt Lake's own gauged inflow record. Caveat: these three gauges capture the main surface tributaries but not ungauged inflow, direct precipitation on the lake or groundwater, and they measure post-depletion flow (already net of upstream diversions), so the series mixes hydrologic variability with changing consumptive use.
verification: curl of the four documented query URLs to local .rdb files, then computed with python3 -I (scripts at scratchpad/research/calc.py and calc2.py); raw files kept at scratchpad/research/usgs/
finding: Combined annual mean discharge of gauges 10126000, 10141000 and 10170490, 1950-2025 (n=69): mean 1,875,736 acre-feet/yr, standard deviation 1,189,548 acre-feet/yr, coefficient of variation 0.634.
strengthWhy: Primary gauged record of the exact quantity the parameter describes, computed directly. Strongest possible evidence class. It contradicts the model's value: measured CV is 0.63, roughly 1.8x the assumed 0.35, so the model understates year-to-year inflow variability. Even the single least variable gauge (Bear River, 0.62) exceeds 0.35.

title: A millennium-length reconstruction of Bear River stream flow, Utah (NOAA/WDS Paleoclimatology data set bear2015flow, Study 19299)
authors: R.J. DeRose, M.F. Bekker, S.-Y. Wang, B.M. Buckley, R.K. Kjelgren, T. Bardsley, T.M. Rittenour, E.B. Allen
place: Bear River headwaters (USGS gauge 10011500), Utah - largest tributary of the Great Salt Lake
publisher: Journal of Hydrology 529(2):524-534, doi:10.1016/j.jhydrol.2015.01.014; data archived by NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
finding: "The most severe period of reduced stream flow occurred during the Medieval Warm Period (ca. mid-1200s CE) and persisted for ~70 years." "The latter half of the 20th century was found to be the 2nd wettest (~40-year) period of the past 1200 years, while the first half of the 20th century marked the 4th driest period."
location: Abstract in the data file header (lines 48-49); value computed from the data block, columns age_AD and flow-rec-m3s, years 800-2010
conversion: Parsed the 1211 annual values of flow-rec-m3s (reconstructed mean annual discharge, m3/s) with python3 -I (script scratchpad/research/pal.py). Full-record mean 4.8 m3/s. Driest running means, as a ratio to that mean: 20-yr 0.694 (1245-1264), 30-yr 0.752 (1232-1261), 50-yr 0.789 (1230-1279), 70-yr 0.821 (1212-1281). The 30-year figure, 0.752, is the one quoted. No unit conversion needed since the parameter is a dimensionless multiplier.
strengthWhy: Peer-reviewed tree-ring reconstruction of the Great Salt Lake's own largest tributary, 1200 years long, calibrated against the gauged record (67% of variance explained), measuring exactly the quantity the parameter encodes: multi-decade mean flow as a fraction of long-run mean. The driest 30-year window is 0.752 of the millennial mean, matching the assumed 0.75 almost exactly. One caveat that cuts the other way: because 1950-2000 was 1.159x the millennial mean in this same series, a megadrought measured against a modern baseline implies a harsher multiplier of about 0.752/1.159 = 0.65, so 0.75 may be optimistic if the model's mean inflow is calibrated on post-1950 data.
differencesFromUtah: None geographically - this is the Bear River itself. It reconstructs headwater flow at gauge 10011500 rather than total inflow to the lake, and tree-ring reconstructions smooth extremes, so single-year minima are understated even though multi-decade means are the reconstruction's strength.
verification: curl of the NOAA data file to scratchpad/research/paleo/bear2015flow.txt; abstract quoted verbatim from the file header; running means computed with python3 -I

title: Mono Lake Fact Sheet (Water Right Decision 1631: target lake level and timeline)
authors: Division of Water Rights staff
publisher: California State Water Resources Control Board
finding: "The board determined that the lake should reach the target lake level within 20 years. This was based on models that estimated how long it could reasonably take for the lake to recover to 6,392 feet." "Mono Lake has not exceeded 6,384 feet since D-1931 [sic] was adopted in 1994... As of December 2022, the lake was at approximately 6,378 feet."
location: pages 2-3, sections 'Water Right Decision 1631' (Target lake level; Timeline) and 'Ongoing developments'
unit: share of the remaining gap per year
conversion: The Board's hydrologic models put ~20 years on closing the gap from the 1994 level (about 6,375-6,377 ft) to the 6,392 ft equilibrium. Treating that as exponential approach, level(t) = target - gap*(1-k)^t: k = 1 - (1-f)^(1/20), so closing 90% of the gap in 20 years implies k = 0.111 and closing 95% implies k = 0.139. The assumed 0.12 closes 92% in 20 years, i.e. it sits inside the band the Board's own 20-year modelled recovery implies. A cross-check on the decline side: the fact sheet states diversions 'caused the lake to decline by 45 feet between 1941 and 1982' (page 1), 41 years for a ~45 ft fall toward a much lower equilibrium, again a decadal, not annual, adjustment timescale.
strengthWhy: Same mechanism - a saline, closed-basin terminal lake responding to a legally mandated step change in inflow - and the figure is an agency's own calibrated hydrologic model of time-to-equilibrium, not an analogy. Marked down from 5 because 20 years is a modelled expectation, not a measured response: the observed outcome is that after 28 years Mono Lake was still about 14 ft below target and had trended downward since 2006, so 0.12/yr is, if anything, faster than the real world delivered once hydrologic variability and continued diversions are included.
differencesFromUtah: Mono Lake is far smaller (about 70 sq mi versus roughly 1,700 sq mi at historic GSL levels) and much deeper, with a snowmelt Sierra inflow and a single diverter under a public-trust court ruling, so its surface-area-to-volume geometry and its politics both differ. A shallower, broader lake like the Great Salt Lake loses proportionally more to evaporation as it rises, which should make its own k smaller (slower approach) than Mono's.
verification: WebFetch returned the raw PDF; converted with pdftotext -layout and quoted verbatim from the extracted text (scratchpad/research/mono.txt, lines 23, 55-62, 82-84)

title: Dust in the Wind: The Health Costs of Great Salt Lake Desiccation (NBER Working Paper 35270)
authors: Lena Harris, Eric C. Edwards, Danae Hernandez-Cortes
finding: "Marginal annual costs range from $81 to $175 million per 100 km2 of exposed lakebed. Scaling to the area of total exposed lakebed, annual desiccation-related health cost estimates range from $1.1 billion to $2.3 billion."
location: abstract, NBER working paper landing page
conversion: Midpoint of the paper's own stated range $1.1bn-$2.3bn/yr of desiccation-related health cost at the current exposed lakebed area = $1.7bn/yr. The marginal form, $81-175 million per 100 km2 exposed (about $0.81-1.75 million per km2 per year), is the figure to use if the model needs damage as a function of exposed area rather than a single total.
strengthWhy: Measured for the Great Salt Lake itself, econometrically linking exposed lakebed area to PM2.5 and then to health costs, so the mechanism and the place both match exactly. Two caveats: it is an unrefereed NBER working paper, and other Utah studies are far lower - a University of Utah Wilkes Center estimate puts current annual health cost near $115 million - so the literature spans an order of magnitude and the model should treat this as an upper-range estimate.
differencesFromUtah: None; it is Utah. It covers dust-driven PM2.5 health cost only, not arsenic or other lakebed toxics, and not non-health losses (ski industry, brine shrimp, mineral extraction, property values).
